title: EU and Azerbaijan advance cooperation at third High-Level Transport Dialogue
source_name: 欧盟委员会交通与运输总司
content: On 26 November, the European Commission and the Ministry of Digital Development and Transport of Azerbaijan met in Baku for the third High-Level Transport Dialogue, co-chaired by Minister Rashad Nabiyev and Director-General Magda Kopczyńska. The dialogue took place at a moment of broader engagement in EU–Azerbaijan relations. It contributed to the Cross-Regional Connectivity Agenda, a flagship of the EU's Strategic Approach to the Black Sea region linking Europe with Central Asia, through the South Caucasus. The dialogue covered key areas of cooperation in all modes of transport. Discussions centred on regional connectivity and aviation relations in particular, in light of Azerbaijan’s strategic role as a bridge between Central Asia and Europe along the Middle Corridor. On connectivity, both sides took stock of progress on the corridor's priority infrastructure, including the Port of Baku and the Nakhchivan railway, and agreed on the need to explore potential updates to the extended TEN-T network in Azerbaijan to reflect recent developments and regional connectivity initiatives in the region. On aviation, the dialogue covered the state of play of the negotiations of the EU–Azerbaijan Common Aviation Area Agreement and the required next steps towards its conclusion. Other areas of discussion include digitalisation, sustainable aviation fuels, and rail interoperability. At today's dialogue, the two sides reaffirmed their commitment to further deepening EU–Azerbaijan transport cooperation in support of a more efficient, resilient and sustainable Middle Corridor. As next steps, the two sides agreed to intensify regular exchanges on the topics discussed, while in particular following up at technical level on the indicative extension of TEN-T maps for Azerbaijan and continue work towards finalising the EU–Azerbaijan Common Aviation Area Agreement. The next transport dialogue, to be held in Brussels in 2027, will provide a moment to take stock of progress achieved in all areas of close cooperation. - Publication date - 26 November 2026 - Author - Directorate-General for Mobility and Transport

title: Technical Updates to the RCRA Hazardous Waste Permitting Regulations-Permitting Technical Updates Rule
content: ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY 40 CFR Parts 124, 260, 261, 262, 263, 264, 265, 266, 267, 268, 270, 271, 273, and 279 [EPA-HQ-OLEM-2024-0124; FRL-9376-01-OLEM] RIN 2050-AH30 Technical Updates to the RCRA Hazardous Waste Permitting Regulations—Permitting Technical Updates Rule AGENCY: Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). ACTION: Proposed rule. SUMMARY: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is proposing technical updates to the regulations implementing the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) governing hazardous waste treatment, storage, and disposal facilities (TSDFs), as well as associated permitting requirements. The proposal also includes a few conforming technical updates to the generator and transporter regulations. The RCRA hazardous waste TSDF permitting regulations have remained largely unchanged for over three decades, despite evolving standards and practices. Collectively, these revisions are intended to address inadvertent errors, remove obsolete references, reflect current information and standards, and implement targeted updates to the RCRA permitting regulations to improve clarity, consistency, and efficiency in the hazardous waste TSDF permitting program. Through a separate Federal Register document, EPA will be seeking input on areas in the RCRA permitting program and permitting regulations to consider for permitting policy or regulatory reform. This proposed rule helps clear the way for potential future regulatory actions that could improve implementation of the RCRA hazardous waste permitting program. It serves as a maintenance action and does not preclude the possibility of future permitting reform. DATES: Comments must be received on or before December 28, 2026. Public Participation Written Comments Submit your comments, identified by Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OLEM-2024-0124, at https://www.regulations.gov (our preferred method), or the other methods identified in the ADDRESSES section. Once submitted, comments cannot be edited or removed from the docket. EPA may publish any comment received to its public docket. EPA will generally not consider comments or comment contents located outside of the primary submission ( i.e., on the web, cloud, or other file sharing system). Please visit https://www.epa.gov/dockets/commenting-epa-dockets for additional submission methods; the full EPA public comment policy; information about CBI, PBI, or multimedia submissions; and general guidance on making effective comments. For the reader's convenience, EPA has provided a background description of existing requirements in several places throughout this preamble. In the absence of a specific request for comment and proposed change to the identified provisions, these descriptions do not reopen any of the described provisions nor reconsider the underlying regulations. The scope of this proposal is limited to the changes specifically identified and EPA is not reconsidering, reopening, or soliciting comment on other RCRA regulations. Due to the length and complexity of the proposal, EPA requests that commenters identify the relevant topic and section number in their comments by using comments codes. For example, use “PM-6b” for section V.A.6 Permit Modification comments for V.A.6.b. Notification of Modification Requests. The codes are given at the end of each section. Through this action, EPA is soliciting comment on targeted technical updates. EPA will be seeking input on topics for RCRA permitting reform through a separate Federal Register document. II. General Information A. Does this action apply to me? This action applies to owners and operators of facilities that treat, store, or dispose of hazardous waste. A small subset of proposed changes which relate to the land disposal restriction regulations and requirements relating to contingency planning, incident reporting, and manifesting would also apply to generators of hazardous waste. In addition, a small subset of proposed changes which relate to transfer facilities would also apply to transporters of hazardous waste. The following list of North American Industrial Classification System (NAICS) codes is not intended to be exhaustive, but rather provides a guide to help readers determine whether this document applies to them. Potentially affected entities may include: (NAICS codes) 562—Waste Management and Remediation Services; 325—Chemical Manufacturing; 928—National Security and International Affairs; 331—Primary Metal Manufacturing; 324—Petroleum and Coal Products Manufacturing; 332—Fabricated Metal Product Manufacturing; 336—Transportation Equipment Manufacturing; 321—Wood Product Manufacturing; 424—Merchant Wholesalers, Nondurable Goods; 327—Nonmetallic Mineral Product Manufacturing; 611—Educational Services; 334—Computer and Electronic Product Manufacturing; 541—Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services; 221—Utilities; 333—Machinery Manufacturing; and, 339—Miscellaneous Manufacturing. To determine whether your entity is affected by this action, you should carefully examine the proposed changes to the regulatory text, as well as applicability provisions in 40 CFR parts 124, 260, 261, 262, 263, 264, 265, 266, 267, 268, 270, 271, 273, and 279. If you have questions regarding the applicability of this action to a particular entity, consult the person listed in the FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT section. B. What action is the Agency taking? EPA is proposing various technical updates to the RCRA hazardous waste treatment, storage, disposal and permitting standards. These proposed changes intend to reflect current information or standards, improve understanding and compliance with the regulations, and make over 400 technical corrections and other conforming changes to address inadvertent errors and remove obsolete references. Please note that in this proposal, EPA is not reconsidering, proposing to reopen, or otherwise soliciting comment on any other provisions of the existing RCRA regulations beyond those specifically identified in this proposal. At the same time, this action does not preclude the possibility of future permitting reform to improve implementation of the RCRA hazardous waste permitting program. C. What is the Agency's authority for taking this action? EPA is proposing these regulations under the authority of sections 1006, 2002(a), 3002, 3003, 3004, 3005, 3010, 3013, and 7004 of the Solid Waste Disposal Act of 1970, as amended by the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act of 1976, as amended, by the Hazardous and Solid Waste Amendments of 1984 (HSWA), 42 U.S.C. 6905, 6912(a), 6922, 6923, 6924, 6925, 6930, 6934, and 6974. These public laws combined are commonly referred to as the “Resource Conservation and Recovery Act” (RCRA) and will be referred to as such for the remainder of this document. RCRA section 1006 provides EPA with the authority to integrate RCRA's requirements with other Acts. Section 2002(a) provides EPA the general authority to prescribe regulations to carry out the functions of RCRA. Section 3002 provides EPA the authority to establish standards applicable to generators of hazardous waste. Section 3003 provides EPA the authority to establish standards applicable to transporters of hazardous waste. Section 3004 provides EPA the authority to establish standards applicable to owners and operators of facilities for the treatment, storage, or disposal of hazardous waste. Section 3005 provides EPA the authority to establish regulations requiring each person owning or operating a hazardous waste treatment, storage, and disposal facility (TSDF) to have a permit. Section 3010 makes regulations promulgated pursuant to RCRA effective in the manner described in the Act. Section 3014 provides EPA with the authority to require monitoring, testing, or analysis for hazardous waste. Section 7004 provides EPA with the authority to review petitions as well as to require and develop standards for public participation. D. What are the incremental costs and benefits of this action? Based on the universe of affected facilities, permits, and activities, as well as the estimated labor and non-labor costs associated with complying with the provisions of the proposed rule, EPA estimates that the universe of permitted facilities and new applicants, on average, will have a total of approximately $0.42 million per year (2025 dollars) in labor and non-labor cost savings (under a 3 percent discount rate). In addition, permitting authorities are expected to realize annual cost savings of $0.50 million (2025 dollars, under a 3 percent discount rate). The annualized cost savings of the proposed rule for permitted facilities, new applicants, and permitting authorities combined are $0.92 million per year (2025 dollars, under a 3 percent discount rate). For a detailed description of costs and benefits of regulatory revisions proposed in this action, refer to the Economic Assessment available in the docket. III. Background When the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act was enacted in 1976, Congress recognized that hazardous waste should be treated, stored, or disposed of in a manner that minimizes present and future threats to human health and the environment. To address these risks, EPA promulgated extensive technical standards for the design and safe operation of hazardous waste management units (HWMUs) at TSDFs. These standards are codified in Title 40 of the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) parts 124 and 260 through 279. Parts 270 and 124 provide requirements pertaining to the hazardous waste permitting process. 1 Part 264 sets minimum national standards for managing hazardous waste at fully permitted TSDFs, while requirements for interim status facilities are included in part 265. 2 Most changes being proposed in this action are located in parts 264, 265, and 270. 1 Unless otherwise noted, the references to “parts” or “sections”(“§ ”) in this preamble are to Title 40 of the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR); for example, “part 270” means 40 CFR part 270. Regulatory requirements for TSDFs are laid out in part 264 and provide the framework and technical standards used to develop a site-specific RCRA permit. 2 RCRA “interim status” allows existing hazardous waste TSDFs to operate while their permit is processed if they were in existence on the effective date of the applicable regulations, notified EPA (or the authorized state), and submitted a timely Part A application, and they comply with interim-status standards ( e.g., part 265). Interim status continues until a final permit is issued or denied, or it terminates for noncompliance or other applicable reasons. This action also proposes revisions to parts that are not core to hazardous waste permitting: parts 124, 260, 261, 262, 263, 266, 267, 268, 271, 273, and 279. Revisions to these parts are included in this proposal because standards and requirements described in these parts may be referenced by the RCRA permit, or because conforming changes in these parts would be needed to ensure consistency with revisions to the TSDF and/or permitting regulations. Part 124 describes the general requirement to obtain a RCRA permit and defines public notice requirements. Part 260 includes general provisions relating to the hazardous waste management system under RCRA, including definitions that apply to parts 260-273. Part 261 discusses identification and listing of hazardous waste. Part 262 describes standards applicable to generators of hazardous waste. Part 263 describes standards applicable to transporters of hazardous waste. Parts 266 and 267 discuss standards that apply to specific activities, types of waste, or types of waste management facilities; these standards often include provisions that must be cited in the operating permit. Part 268 describes land disposal restrictions that apply to TSDFs, as well as other regulated entities. Part 271 describes requirements for the authorization of state hazardous waste programs. Part 273 describes the standards for universal waste management. Part 279 describes the standards for the management of used oil. Permitted facilities. TSDFs are required to obtain a permit, which provides TSDF owners and operators with the legal authority to treat, store, or dispose of hazardous waste and details how the facility must comply with the regulations. The permit is a legally binding document that establishes the administrative and technical conditions under which hazardous waste at the facility must be managed. In this document, the term “permit” generally refers to the RCRA TSDF permits described here, unless otherwise specified. Permits also serve as an implementation mechanism and as a means by which EPA can track waste management at facilities that handle hazardous waste. Owners and operators of facilities that do not comply with permit provisions are subject to RCRA enforcement actions, including financial penalties. Permits can be issued by EPA or authorized state RCRA programs. The permitting authority and TSDF owners or operators engage with each other throughout all stages of the permitting process, from preparation of the permit application, through permit issuance, including permit modifications and renewals, until permit termination. The process also includes public participation at each stage, as applicable. For new TSDFs seeking a permit, and facilities seeking a permit renewal, the owner and operator must submit a comprehensive permit application that addresses all applicable regulatory standards, including general facility provisions, unit-specific requirements, closure and post-closure requirements, financial assurance standards, and any applicable groundwater monitoring and air emissions provisions. The permit application must demonstrate that the permittee's methods of handling the waste are consistent with the level of protection of human health and the environment required by RCRA. The permit application is divided into two parts, Part A and Part B. The Part A application requires basic information about the facility. The Part B application includes site-specific information associated with the waste management activities that will be conducted at the facility, such as chemical and physical analyses of the hazardous waste, and includes geologic, hydrologic, and engineering data. This process provides a mechanism for the permitting authority to request additional information through a notice of deficiency and includes an opportunity for public review and comment. Ultimately, the permitting authority makes the decision to issue or deny the permit. EPA views permits as living documents that can be modified to allow facilities to implement technological improvements, comply with new environmental standards, respond to changing waste streams or conditions, and generally improve waste management practices. Once a permit has been issued, changes may be necessary. Permit modification procedures provide owners and operators and the permitting authority with flexibility to change permit conditions, with public notification and participation, as applicable. Interim status facilities. Many TSDFs were already in existence and operating when they became subject to RCRA regulatory requirements as a result of a statutory or regulatory change. These owners and operators were immediately subject to the RCRA requirements, including the requirement to obtain an operating permit. Such facilities were allowed to obtain “interim status,” which allowed them to continue operating until they were either issued a permit or until applicable closure and post-closure responsibilities are fulfilled. Under interim status, a facility can operate without a permit as long as it complies with certain general facility and unit-specific TSDF standards in 40 CFR part 265, until the permitting agency makes a final permit determination. Currently, fewer than 10 facilities are operating under interim status and actively managing hazardous waste. Through this action, the Agency is proposing several technical updates to address inadvertent errors and remove obsolete references; reflect current information and standards; and incrementally improve clarity, consistency, and efficiency in the hazardous waste TSDF permitting program. IV. Methodology EPA developed this proposal from ideas compiled from numerous sources over several years regarding potential revisions to the RCRA permitting regulations. While some cited materials are older, the issues they address remain current. The primary source of potential revisions was through ongoing implementation of the RCRA hazardous waste permitting program, wherein issues and suggestions for improvement from EPA implementation staff, authorized state and territories, and regulated entities have been collected and documented over time. Many of these items have been previously considered and clarified by EPA through issuance of program guidance and policy available publicly on the EPA website and RCRA Online. 3 3 RCRA Online is an electronic database that indexes thousands of letters, memoranda, publications, and questions and answers issued by EPA's Office of Resource Conservation and Recovery (ORCR). These documents represent past EPA Headquarters interpretations of the RCRA regulations governing the management of solid, hazardous, and medical waste. Available at: https://rcrapublic.epa.gov/rcraonline/. Additional sources included issues identified by the Office of Enforcement and Compliance Assurance (OECA) through EPA's National Enforcement and Compliance Initiative to Reduce Hazardous Air Emissions for Hazardous Waste Facilities; regulatory revisions made in previous EPA rulemakings, such as EPA's 2016 Generator Improvements Rule (81 FR 85732, November 28, 2016); public comments received through the Executive Order (E.O.) Enforcing the Regulatory Reform Agenda (E.O. 13777 4 of February 24, 2017); and numerous technical corrections received from a firm that delivers training on the RCRA regulations. 4 The E.O. was revoked on January 20, 2021, through E.O. 13992 (86 FR 7049). However, the feedback received in response to this order continues to be relevant and informative. V. Discussion of Proposed Changes EPA's proposed changes focus mainly on the RCRA hazardous waste treatment, storage, and disposal, and permitting regulations, in 40 CFR parts 264, 265, and 270. Additionally, this action proposes changes to regulations located in other parts of the CFR related to hazardous waste permitting, transportation, and generation, located in parts 124, 260, 261, 262, 263, 266, 267, 268, 271, 273, and 279. EPA is requesting comment on each of the proposed changes discussed in the following subsections, which include proposed changes to clarify language, codify longstanding policy, update standards, and make technical corrections. EPA will use the public comments it receives to make decisions on whether and how to finalize revisions. To assist public commenter's review, EPA has included two files in the docket to aid in review of this relatively large proposal: • “List of Preamble Topics and Regs Covered.pdf.” • “Redline Comparison Between Existing and Proposed Regulation Changes.pdf.” First, the document titled “List of Preamble Topics and Regs Covered” lists each topic in the preamble and the regulations covered in each topic. There are hundreds of paragraphs in the regulations that are being revised, and a regulation can be revised for more than one preamble topic. Second, the document titled “Redline Comparison Between Existing and Proposed Regulation Changes” presents the proposed changes in a red-line format compared to the existing regulations. Public commenters may find this red-line document particularly helpful in understanding how EPA is proposing to amend the regulations. A. Technical Updates EPA is proposing several changes to improve the clarity of various regulatory provisions, reflect current information and standards, enhance clarity, consistency, and efficiency in the hazardous waste TSDF permitting program, and update references to standards established by regulatory programs other than RCRA that are incorporated into the RCRA regulations. These changes are supported by existing policy and analysis established or communicated in EPA memoranda, guidance, or other documents. This section describes proposed changes organized by the following subjects: • Permit application (V.A.1), • Preparedness and prevention, contingency plan and emergency procedures (V.A.2), • Financial assurance (V.A.3), • RCRA organic air emission standards (V.A.4), • General language clarification (V.A.5), • Permit modification (V.A.6), • Modernizing public notice (V.A.7), • Location standards regulatory comments (V.A.8), • Transfer facility storage period (V.A.9), • Drip pads (V.A.10). 1. Permit Application EPA is proposing several changes relating to permit applications for initial permits and permit renewals. The permit application consists of two parts: Part A and Part B. Part A includes basic facility information, such as location, contact information, and process descriptions. Part B of the RCRA permit application contains both general and specific information that is necessary for EPA to assess whether the applicant will be in compliance with the regulatory standards outlined in 40 CFR part 264. Part B is comprehensive and may contain technical data, drawings, studies, and other descriptive or analytical information, which is the main focus of this section. The proposed changes described in this section aim to ensure that permit applications provide permitting authorities with the complete information necessary to process RCRA permit applications effectively. The permitting authority needs this information before drafting permit conditions that, if followed, promote compliance with the regulations and protect human health and the environment over the permit term. A permit application must be complete and technically adequate for the permitting authority to conduct a thorough evaluation. For further details, refer to 40 CFR 124.3(a)(2). Incomplete or insufficient permit applications are a major factor contributing to delays in issuing RCRA permits and renewals. When an incomplete or technically inadequate permit application is submitted, both the permitting authority(ies) and permittee often have to invest significant time and resources to gather the necessary details. This process can involve discussions, requests for additional information, and multiple reviews of resubmitted applications. According to a report by the Association of State and Territorial Solid Waste Management Officials (ASTSWMO), 5 application review accounted for 25% of the total permitting program costs borne by states, surpassing the costs associated with permit issuance, which stood at 21% (while this is from an older report, it is still relevant and informative). EPA anticipates that the proposed clarifications to the regulations will enhance the initial quality and completeness of permit applications. This improvement should reduce the number of iterations required, thereby shortening the overall time needed to complete the permitting process. 5 ASTSWMO is an organization representing the 50 States, 5 Territories and the District of Columbia. ASTSWMO published a report January 22, 2007: “State RCRA Subtitle C Core Hazardous Waste Management Program Implementation Costs,” available at: https://astswmo.org/state-rcra-subtitle-c-core-hazardous-waste-management-program-implementation-costs/. This is also referred to as the “2007 ASTSWMO Core Report.” The proposed revisions focus on the following permit-application topics: • Permit application information and technical requirements, and • Permit application submittal timeframe. EPA is requesting comment on the following proposed changes. a. Permit Application Information and Technical Requirements EPA is proposing revisions to several regulatory provisions that reference the application requirements and list the CFR Parts containing technical requirements to be addressed in the application. These proposed revisions are described below for §§ 124.3(a)(2), 270.2, 270.10(c), 270.10(d), 270.14(a), 270.51(a)(1). Additionally, similar updates to § 270.1(a)(3) are discussed. EPA emphasizes that none of the proposed changes concerning information and technical requirements will limit the permitting authority's ability, allowed under current regulations, to request additional information during the permit drafting process. According to the existing regulations in § 124.3(c), even after an application is deemed complete, the Regional Administrator may request further information from an applicant, but only when necessary to clarify, modify, or supplement previously submitted material. Such requests for additional information will not render an application incomplete. EPA is proposing to amend § 124.3(a)(2) to reference the full scope of RCRA permit application requirements. Currently, § 124.3(a)(2) outlines the information needed for the permitting authority to begin processing a permit application, but it only references §§ 270.10 (General application requirements) and 270.13 (Contents of Part A of the permit application), which represent just a portion of the applicable requirements. To address this, EPA is proposing to add references to § 270.14 (Contents of Part B; General requirements), and §§ 270.15 through 270.28 (Specific Part B information requirements), as applicable. title: Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards: Automatic Emergency Braking Systems for Light Vehicles
content: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION National Highway Traffic Safety Administration 49 CFR Part 571 [Docket No. NHTSA-2026-2476] RIN 2127-AM69 Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards: Automatic Emergency Braking Systems for Light Vehicles AGENCY: National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), U.S. Department of Transportation (Department or DOT). ACTION: Notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM). SUMMARY: NHTSA proposes to modify Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard No. 127; Automatic emergency braking systems for light vehicles. NHTSA proposes to delay the compliance date by two years so that manufacturers have more time to comply with the standard. NHTSA also proposes test procedures for testing the malfunction telltale and to clarify the test speed tolerance. The agency seeks comment on other potential modifications to the standard. DATES: Comments must be received on or before January 26, 2027. Proposed compliance date: Compliance would be required for all vehicles manufactured on or after September 1, 2031. Small-volume manufacturers, final-stage manufacturers, and alterers would be provided an additional year, with compliance required for all vehicles manufactured by such entities on or after September 1, 2032. Regulatory Notices and Analyses VII. Public Participation VIII. Regulatory Text I. Executive Summary A. Background and Summary of FMVSS No. 127 The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA), enacted in November 2021, 1 mandated that the Secretary of Transportation promulgate a rule to establish minimum performance standards with respect to crash avoidance technology and to require that all passenger motor vehicles manufactured for sale in the United States be equipped with forward collision warning (FCW) and automatic emergency braking (AEB) systems that alert the driver if a collision is imminent and apply the brakes automatically if the driver fails to do so. In addition, under the authority of the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act of 1966 (Safety Act), 2 the Secretary of Transportation is charged with establishing Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS) that are practicable, meet the need for motor vehicle safety, and are stated in objective terms. The authority to issue FMVSSs is delegated to NHTSA. 3 1 Public Law 117-58. 2 The Safety Act is codified at 49 U.S.C. Chapter 301. 3 49 CFR 1.93(a). NHTSA issued a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) on June 13, 2023, followed by a final rule on May 9, 2024, establishing a new FMVSS No. 127, “Automatic Emergency Braking Systems for Light Vehicles.” 4 FMVSS No. 127 requires all passenger cars, multipurpose passenger vehicles, trucks, and buses with a gross vehicle weight rating (GVWR) less than 4,536 kg (10,000 lbs) manufactured on or after September 1, 2029 to be equipped with forward collision warning (FCW), automatic emergency braking (AEB), and pedestrian automatic emergency braking (PAEB) technology. On November 26, 2024, NHTSA issued a final rule in response to petitions for reconsideration that made clarifying amendments to the standard but largely denied the petitions. 5 The Alliance for Automotive Innovation (Alliance) subsequently filed a challenge to FMVSS No. 127 in the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit on January 17, 2025. 6 4 89 FR 39686 (May 9, 2024). 5 89 FR 93199 (Nov. 26, 2024). 6 The United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, Case No.: 25-1026. https://www.autosinnovate.org/posts/testimony/Auto%20Innovators%20AEB%20Petition%20Filing.pdf, accessed March 2026. FMVSS No. 127 includes four requirements for AEB systems to warn of and brake for both lead vehicles and pedestrians. The AEB system must: (1) provide an FCW consisting of auditory and visual warning of an impending collision with a lead vehicle at any forward speed greater than 10 km/h (6.2 mph) and less than 145 km/h (90 mph) and an FCW of an impending collision with a pedestrian at any forward speed greater than 10 km/h (6.2 mph) and less than 73 km/h (45.3 mph), (2) apply the brakes automatically at any forward speed greater 10 km/h (6.2 mph) and less than 145 km/h (90 mph) when a collision with a lead vehicle is imminent and at any forward speed greater than 10 km/h (6.2 mph) and less than 73 km/h (45.3 mph) when a collision with a pedestrian is imminent; (3) prevent the vehicle from colliding with the lead vehicle or pedestrian test device when tested according to the test procedures described in the standard, which include pedestrian tests in both daylight and darkness, and pass two false positive tests; and (4) provide telltale notification if the system detects a malfunction, or if the system adjusts its performance such that it will not meet the requirements of the standard. Compliance is required starting September 1, 2029, with applicable vehicles manufactured by small-volume manufacturers, final-stage manufacturers, and alterers required to be certified to the standard by September 1, 2030. FMVSS No. 127 addresses significant safety problems. AEB systems employ sensor technologies and sub-systems that work together to sense when the vehicle is in a crash imminent situation, provide a warning to the driver and apply the vehicle brakes automatically if the driver has not done so, and to apply more braking force to supplement the driver's braking, to avoid or mitigate a collision. These systems can reduce the frequency and severity of both lead vehicle rear-end and pedestrian collisions. As outlined in the 2024 final rule, in 2019, 60 percent of fatal rear-end crashes and 73 percent of crashes resulting in injuries were on roads with posted speed limits of 60 mph or below, and the vast majority of fatalities, injuries, and property damage associated with rear end crashes occur at speeds above 25 mph. Similarly, most of these crashes occurred without adverse atmospheric conditions: 72 percent of fatal crashes and 74 percent of crashes resulting in injuries occurred in clear conditions. Also, about 51 percent of fatal rear-end crashes and 74 percent of rear-end crashes resulting in injuries involving light vehicles occurred in daylight conditions. In addition, 65 percent of pedestrian fatalities and 67 percent of pedestrian injuries were the result of a strike by the front of a light vehicle. About half of pedestrian injuries and 77 percent of pedestrian fatalities occurred in dark lighting conditions. FMVSS No. 127 establishes test scenarios for both lead vehicle and pedestrian AEB systems. Lead vehicle AEB is tested at speeds up to 100 km/h (62 mph) when manual braking is applied and up to 80 km/h (50 mph) when no manual braking is applied during the test. Lead vehicle testing is performed under three representative scenarios: lead vehicle stopped, lead vehicle moving, and lead vehicle decelerating. PAEB is tested only without manual braking and at speeds up to 65 km/h (40 mph). PAEB testing is performed under three representative scenarios: pedestrian crossing the road (including an obstructed pedestrian scenario), stationary pedestrian (in the path of the vehicle), and pedestrian moving along the vehicle path. Because most pedestrian fatalities occur in darkness, PAEB performance is required under both daylight and darkness lighting conditions. The Final Regulatory Impact Analysis for FMVSS No. 127 concluded the rule would result in a reduction of 362 fatalities and 24,321 injuries annually. The total costs of the rule were estimated to be approximately $354 million annually, most of which was attributable to the installation of software. However, NHTSA estimated that approximately five percent of the light vehicle fleet would require hardware upgrades to existing FCW and AEB systems to meet FMVSS No. 127. The lifetime monetized net benefits of the rule were projected to be between $5.82 and $7.26 billion. As discussed in the remainder of the preamble, there is uncertainty as to whether rule-compliant AEB can be implemented throughout the fleet within the prescribed timeline, and, therefore, whether the projected fatality and injury reductions, and thus these projected benefits, would accrue as estimated in the 2024 final rule and accompanying Final Regulatory Impact Analysis. B. Summary of This NPRM This NPRM proposes a two-year delay in the compliance timeline for FMVSS No. 127. In the time since the finalization of FMVSS No. 127, NHTSA has continued to conduct both lead vehicle and pedestrian AEB testing as part of the New Car Assessment Program (NCAP) program, largely to the specifications in FMVSS No. 127. In addition, NHTSA has met with several stakeholders, some of whom have challenged whether the standard is practicable, meets the need for safety, and is stated in objective terms. This information is summarized in Section II of this proposed rule. Based on the information received from stakeholders and developed by NHTSA through additional testing, NHTSA has determined that there is uncertainty in whether the fleet can comply with the standard within the current compliance timeline. There is also uncertainty around the pace of system development and deployment, and how the current compliance timeline might impact engineering and marketing decisions made years in advance of vehicle sales. As a result, NHTSA is concerned that the current timeline of FMVSS No. 127 may result in vehicles being unable to be self-certified as compliant by manufacturers, and therefore prohibited from sale. Consequently, NHTSA has determined that the current compliance date, September 1, 2029, may be impracticable for the fleet. The agency also seeks comment on the practicability and stringency of several aspects of FMVSS No. 127. This standard is more stringent than AEB regulations developed by other countries, and uncertainty remains regarding how several aspects of the standard will impact AEB performance in the field and consumer response to that performance, both in the short and long term. This consideration applies to several aspects of the rule, but particularly to the “no contact” requirement, the required test speeds, and the lack of multiple test trials. NHTSA is concerned that AEB system design choices made to conform with FMVSS No. 127 specifications could adversely impact consumer acceptance and introduce the possibility of safety disbenefits centered around unexpected activation of AEB at high speeds. In Section IV of this NPRM, NHTSA seeks comment on potential changes to the standard that may mitigate the risk of consumer acceptance issues while maximizing the safety benefits from AEB systems. NHTSA emphasizes that data that might enable quantification of safety risks from false positive AEB activation and data and research on real-world performance of vehicles relative to the track test performance required by FMVSS No. 127 would be particularly helpful in enabling the agency to determine potential future regulatory amendments that may be warranted. Finally, NHTSA solicits comment on the appropriateness of portions of the standard for vehicles equipped with automated driving systems (ADS). C. Legal Authority This NPRM is issued under the authority in the Safety Act. Pursuant to 49 U.S.C. Chapter 301, the Secretary of Transportation is charged with establishing motor vehicle safety standards that are practicable, meet the need for motor vehicle safety, and are stated in objective terms. “Motor vehicle safety” is defined in the Safety Act as “the performance of a motor vehicle or motor vehicle equipment in a way that protects the public against unreasonable risk of accidents occurring because of the design, construction, or performance of a motor vehicle, and against unreasonable risk of death or injury in a crash and includes nonoperational safety of a motor vehicle.” The phrase “Motor vehicle safety standard” means a minimum performance standard for motor vehicles or motor vehicle equipment. When prescribing such standards, the Secretary must consider all relevant, available motor vehicle safety information. The Secretary must also consider whether a standard is reasonable, practicable, and appropriate for the types of motor vehicles or motor vehicle equipment for which it is prescribed and the extent to which the standard will further the statutory purpose of reducing traffic accidents and associated deaths. The authority to issue FMVSS is delegated to NHTSA. FMVSS No. 127 also addresses a statutory mandate under IIJA, which directed the Secretary of Transportation to promulgate a rule requiring that all passenger motor vehicles for sale in the United States be equipped with a FCW system and an AEB system. 7 7 IIJA, Public Law 117-58, Section 24208, codified as 49 U.S.C. 30129. The Safety Act requires that FMVSS be practicable, meet the need for motor vehicle safety, and be stated in objective terms. To meet the requirement that standards be “practicable,” NHTSA considers several factors, including technological and economic feasibility 8 and consumer acceptance. 9 Technological feasibility considerations counsel against standards for which “many technical problems have been identified and no consensus exists for their resolution.” 10 NHTSA recognizes that setting overly aggressive standards can lead to deployment of technology that has not been developed fully—and with degrees of fullness that can vary widely by manufacturer. Premature deployment of technologies, even with the best of intentions and in the expectation that the technology will advance within the given lead time, can lead to consumer acceptance concerns and potentially create safety risk. This is particularly true with technology that intervenes aggressively in the driving task—such as requiring operation at up to 145 km/h (90 mph) of a technology that has long had problems with false positive AEB activation. Economic feasibility considerations focus on whether the cost on industry to comply with the standard would be prohibitive. Technology-forcing regulations, such as the requirements established in the 2024 rule, create challenges like those present here because it is difficult for a regulator to predict the development and technology investments needed to achieve the standard. 8 See, e.g., Paccar, Inc. v. Nat'l Highway Traffic Safety Admin., 573 F.2d 632, 634 n.5 (“ `Practicable' is defined to require consideration of all relevant factors, including technological ability to achieve the goal of a particular standard as well as consideration of economic factors.”) (citations omitted). 9 Pac. Legal Found. v. Dep't of Transp., 593 F.2d 1338, 1345 (D.C. Cir. 1979) (noting in reference to practicable and meet the need for safety, that “the agency cannot fulfill its statutory responsibility unless it considers popular reaction”). 10 Simms v. Nat'l Highway Traffic Safety Admin., 45 F.3d 999, 1011 (6th Cir. 1995). In establishing FMVSS, NHTSA must also consider consumer acceptance. In particular, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit has noted that “motor vehicle safety standards cannot be considered practicable unless we know . . . that motorists will avail themselves of the safety system. Without public cooperation, there can be no assurance that a safety system can meet the need for motor vehicle safety. And it would be difficult to term `practicable' a system . . . that so annoyed motorists that they deactivated it.” 11 Because of the importance of the AEB system to safety, FMVSS No. 127 does not permit installation of a manual control whose sole function is deactivation of the AEB system. Consumer acceptance, however, can impact purchase decisions. Because recent model year used vehicles can act as ready substitutes for a new vehicle, if an FMVSS forces adoption and application of technology that consumers reject, potential new car buyers may decide to delay any purchase or to purchase an older vehicle. This would have the effect of slowing down the adoption and use of new safety technology. NHTSA understands that if consumers do not accept a required safety technology, the technology will not deliver the safety benefits that NHTSA anticipates. 12 13 11 Pac. Legal Found., 593.F.2d at 1346 [internal quotation marks omitted]. 12 See, 82 FR 3854, 3920. Due to the nature of the technology, consumer acceptance was a key factor discussed in the 2017 NPRM on vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) technology. NHTSA also conducted significant research into consumer acceptance and beliefs about V2V technology. 13 In one of the several cases involving FMVSS No. 208, the D.C. Circuit accepted as a “sufficient explanation” for a change from a prior determination, the DOT Secretary's determination that their different estimate of public resistance to a technology was “a matter of judgment.” Pac. Legal Found., 593.F.2d at 1346. The court noted that the Secretary could reasonably anticipate consumers to be more willing to accept airbags than automatic seatbelts and seatbelt interlocks because, in addition to research which indicated a lower deactivation rate for airbags than interlock systems, airbags are less intrusive and do not require independent action by passengers to activate. This logic was reinforced by the high use rate of non-interlock seat belts, as well as research on the rate of passive seat belt use, air bag deactivation rate, and research suggesting that increased deployment of air bags would not reduce the use rate of seat belts. As NHTSA acknowledged in responses to petitions for reconsideration on the final rule promulgating FMVSS No. 127, there is uncertainty regarding the real-world safety impacts of certain aspects of FMVSS No. 127 due to data limitations regarding false positives and low-speed impacts that limit the precision of some elements of the analysis or leave some aspects unquantified. 14 The obligation to resolve such uncertainties to the extent possible is an integral part of NHTSA's mandate under the Safety Act and the Administrative Procedure Act. 15 As always, NHTSA will consider the data available and apply our expert judgment about the unquantifiable aspects of the rule to select the option that is practicable, stated in objective terms, and meets the need for safety. To assist the agency in resolving the uncertainties to the extent possible and selecting the approaches that are practicable and meet the need for safety, NHTSA requests that, in providing their comments, stakeholders provide research or data to support their assertions that might enable the agency to quantify the safety or consumer acceptance impact of a particular change in a requirement or to quantify the implications of the compliance margins applied by manufacturers to meet specific requirements. 14 89 FR 93199, 93204 and 93206-93207. 15 5 U.S.C. 551 et seq. and § 706. In issuing this proposal, NHTSA is obligated to “examine the relevant data and articulate a satisfactory explanation for its action, including a `rational connection between the facts found and the choice made.' ” 16 This proposal reflects a reevaluation of the existing record and consideration of additional information received by NHTSA since the issuance of FMVSS No. 127. Discussed below, this includes test results from recent model year vehicles using updated test procedures, as well as additional consumer complaint information regarding AEB and FCW systems. NHTSA staff have also met with several stakeholders. 17 NHTSA proposes that additional time is necessary to provide manufacturers adequate lead time to bring to market AEB systems that meet the requirements of FMVSS No. 127 practicably, and without introducing systems that adversely affect consumer acceptance or lead to potential for safety disbenefits. 16 Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n of U.S., Inc. v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 29 (1983) ( State Farm ) (noting that a rule would normally be arbitrary and capricious if “the agency has relied on factors which Congress has not intended it to consider, entirely failed to consider an important aspect of the problem, offered an explanation for its decision that runs counter to the evidence before the agency, or is so implausible that it could not be ascribed to a difference in view or the product of agency expertise.”). 17 Staff from NHTSA met with representatives of The Alliance on March 14, 2025, June 12, 2025, and January 20, 2026, Zendar, Inc. on March 19, 2025, Teledyne Technologies, Inc. on April 30, 2025, and American Honda Motor Co. (Honda) on April 30, 2025. II. Delay of Compliance Date A. Information Developed and Obtained Since Finalization of FMVSS No. 127 1. Data on Vehicle Performance In developing FMVSS No. 127, NHTSA conducted research and testing over several years. NHTSA began testing lead vehicle AEB systems in 2010 and began PAEB research in 2011. 18 The latest testing that informed the 2024 final rule was performed in 2023 on six vehicles and included scenarios and conditions from FMVSS No. 127, as well as testing of other parameters and conditions outside the requirements of FMVSS No. 127. 19 20 When tested to the conditions in FMVSS No. 127, no vehicle avoided contact in all trials conducted—one of the standard's performance requirements. The 2023 Toyota Corolla Hybrid XLE avoided contact in each scenario on most occasions, but contact occurred on some trials. 18 89 FR 39686 (May 9, 2024). 19 The vehicles tested included the 2023 BMW iX, 2023 Ford F-150 Lightning, 2023 Hyundai Ioniq 5 Limited, 2024 Mazda CX-90 Turbo S, 2023 Nissan Pathfinder SL, and the 2023 Toyota Corolla Hybrid XLE. 20 https://www.regulations.gov/document/NHTSA-2023-0021-1068, https://www.regulations.gov/document/NHTSA-2023-0021-1066. Since the issuance of the final rule, NHTSA has been testing vehicles as part of NCAP. At the time of development of this NPRM, NHTSA has collected preliminary results for the following ten model year 2025 21 vehicles: Chevrolet Equinox LT FWD, Ford Expedition Active 4x2, Hyundai Santa Fe Calligraphy 2.5T FWD, Jeep Grand Cherokee Laredo 4x4, Kia K4 GT-Line Turbo, Nissan Rogue SL FWD, Subaru Forester Premium Hybrid/SFE, Toyota 4Runner 4WD SR5, Volkswagen Tiguan S and Volvo XC40 B5 AWD Plus. The final results of these tests will be made available in the NCAP results docket for MY 2025 vehicles (final results may differ slightly from those stated in this NPRM). However, the relevant data is presented in this proposal. 21 In addition to the vehicles discussed in the preamble of this NPRM, NHTSA continues to test additional vehicles as part of the NCAP program. Test reports for these vehicles are placed in a docket accessible through the NHTSA website, which can be found at https://www.nhtsa.gov/ratings/resources-related-nhtsas-new-car-assessment-program#procedures--reports. There are four important limitations of this data. First, as with the vehicles tested for the 2024 final rule, the testing was not intended to be a representative or distributive sample of the fleet regarding class, size, price range, or performance. Therefore, as with the 2024 final rule, caution should be taken in interpreting any vehicle's performance as representative of the entire fleet or of a class of vehicles. Second, given that the requirements of FMVSS No. 127 are not currently in force, manufacturers may not have designed the AEB systems on the tested vehicles to the specifications of that regulation. Third, as with the vehicles tested for the 2024 final rule, the test results reflect only the vehicle tested, and may not indicate the AEB performance of other trim level configurations within the model line. Fourth, even if a vehicle is able to meet performance requirements at times, this alone would not satisfy the internal standards of most manufacturers to enable certification that the vehicle meets the requirements of the standard. Most manufacturers will establish criteria ensuring that all vehicles will meet requirements every time the vehicles are tested—generally providing a “compliance margin” to account for potential variations in testing. In developing this proposed rule, NHTSA made certain inferences based on this data, which is the best and most recent data available to the agency upon which it can base its decision making. 22 22 An example of an area where NHTSA may not be able to obtain conclusive data on AEB performance is related to vehicle weight. Due to the low sample and lack of information on the system design and version, NHTSA has tentatively determined that no relation can be inferred between performance and vehicle weight solely on the test data detailed in this notice. NHTSA seeks comment on how the variation in mass between trim configurations, such as engine and drive train configuration or different bed and cab configurations on pickup trucks, might contribute to AEB performance on a test track in more recent model years. The updated NCAP AEB and PAEB test parameters are substantively similar to those in FMVSS No. 127; however, there are some differences. 23 24 Some of the most notable ones are: 23 The NCAP AEB and PAEB test protocols can be reviewed in detail in the docket accompanying the 2024 NCAP Final Decision Notice—Advanced Driver Assistance Systems and Roadmap (89 FR 95916) (NHTSA-2024-0077). 24 https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-B/chapter-V/part-571/subpart-B/section-571.127, accessed November 16, 2026. 1. All NCAP AEB tests are performed in 10 km/h (6.2 mph) increments at discrete speeds depending on the scenario, while FMVSS No. 127 provides ranges. 2. NCAP AEB testing in the lead vehicle stopped without manual brake application scenario is performed at speeds starting at 40 km/h (24.9 mph) and up to 80 km/h (49.7 mph). In FMVSS No. 127, testing for this scenario is performed within the speed range of 10 km/h (6.2 mph) to 80 km/h (49.7 mph). 3. NCAP PAEB testing is performed at speeds starting at 10 km/h (6.2 mph) and up to 60 km/h (37.3 mph) for all scenarios and involves more testing scenarios than FMVSS No. 127 (the results from testing these additional scenarios are not presented here). For the obstructed pedestrian crossing from the right with a 50 percent overlap, FMVSS No. 127 specifies testing only up to 50 km/h (31.1 mph), and for the stationary pedestrian on the right with a 25 percent overlap, FMVSS No. 127 specifies testing only up to 55 km/h (34.2 mph)—NCAP PAEB 60 km/h (37.3 mph) results are shown here. Further, FMVSS No. 127 specifies testing for pedestrian moving along path on the right at 25 percent overlap to be performed at speeds up to 65 km/h (40.4 mph), while no NCAP PAEB testing result exist for this speed and scenario. 4. NCAP PAEB testing is performed during the daylight and in darkness with only lower beam lighting conditions. FMVSS No. 127 PAEB testing is performed in daylight and in darkness with both lower beam and upper beam lighting conditions. 5. NCAP PAEB testing for the obstructed child pedestrian from the right with 50 percent overlap is more stringent than FMVSS No. 127 for the same scenario. In NCAP, the distance between the vehicle being tested and the obstructing vehicles, or test devices, can be as low as 0.9 m, but no more than 1.1 m.
