title: Air Plan Approval; Utah; Cache County Inspection and Maintenance Program Revision
content: ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY 40 CFR Part 52 [EPA-R08-OAR-2026-4555; FRL-13661-01-R8] Air Plan Approval; Utah; Cache County Inspection and Maintenance Program Revision AGENCY: Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). ACTION: Proposed rule. SUMMARY: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is proposing to approve State Implementation Plan (SIP) revisions submitted by the State of Utah on February 28, 2025. The Utah submittal includes revisions to the State's Administrative Rule R307-110-36, concerning SIP Section X Vehicle Inspection and Maintenance (I/M) Program, Part F, Cache County. These revisions updated the rule effectiveness date, updated the definition of vehicle I/M program stations, added emergency vehicle exemptions, and added a part unavailability waiver to the Cache County, Utah I/M program. DATES: Written comments must be received on or before December 28, 2026. ADDRESSES: Submit your comments, identified by Docket ID No. EPA-R08-OAR-2026-4555, to the Federal Rulemaking Portal: https://www.regulations.gov. Follow the online instructions for submitting comments. Once submitted, comments cannot be edited or removed from https://www.regulations.gov. The EPA may publish any comment received to its public docket. Do not submit electronically any information you consider to be Confidential Business Information (CBI) or other information whose disclosure is restricted by statute. Multimedia submissions (audio, video, etc.) must be accompanied by a written comment. The written comment is considered the official comment and should include discussion of all points you wish to make. The EPA will generally not consider comments or comment contents located outside of the primary submission ( i.e., on the web, cloud, or other file sharing system). For additional submission methods, the full EPA public comment policy, information about CBI or multimedia submissions, and general guidance on making effective comments, please visit https://www.epa.gov/dockets/commenting-epa-dockets. Docket: All documents in the docket are listed in the https://www.regulations.gov index. Although listed in the index, some information is not publicly available, e.g., CBI or other information whose disclosure is restricted by statute. Certain other material, such as copyrighted material, will be publicly available only in hard copy. Publicly available docket materials are available electronically in https://www.regulations.gov. Please email or call the person listed in the FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT section if you need to make alternative arrangements for access to the docket. FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: Gregory Lohrke, Air and Radiation Division, EPA, Region 8, Mailcode 8ARD-IO, 1595 Wynkoop Street, Denver, Colorado 80202-1129; telephone number: (303) 312-6396; email address: lohrke.gregory@epa.gov. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Throughout this document wherever “we,” “us,” or “our” is used, we mean the EPA. We use multiple acronyms and terms in this preamble. While this list may not be exhaustive, to ease the reading of this preamble and for reference purposes, the EPA defines the following terms and acronyms here: APA Administrative Procedure Act BRHD Bear River Health Department CAA Clean Air Act CBI Confidential Business Information CFR Code of Federal Regulations EVFM Emergency Vehicle Field Modification EPA U.S. Environmental Protection Agency FR Federal Register I/M Inspection and Maintenance IBR Incorporation by Reference NAA Nonattainment Area NAAQS National Ambient Air Quality Standards NOX Nitrogen Oxides PM Particulate Matter PM2.5 Fine Particulate Matter SIP State Implementation Plan UAQB Utah Air Quality Board VOC Volatile Organic Compounds Table of Contents I. Executive Summary A. What action is the EPA taking? B. What is the legal authority and what are the requirements? II. Background III. The EPA's Evaluation of the State's Submittal A. Utah's SIP Revision IV. Consideration of CAA Section 110(l) V. Incorporation by Reference VI. Statutory and Executive Order Reviews I. Executive Summary A. What action is the EPA taking? The EPA is proposing to approve Utah's February 28, 2025, SIP revision incorporating recent changes to the Cache County, Utah I/M program. This proposed approval is based on a finding that the revisions to the Cache County I/M program, and subsequent incorporation of those changes into the Utah SIP, would not interfere with any applicable requirement concerning maintenance of the 2006 24-hour particulate matter (PM) with an aerodynamic diameter less than or equal to 2.5 microns (PM 2.5 ) National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) or any other applicable requirement of the Clean Air Act (CAA). B. What is the legal authority and what are the requirements? Under section 109 of the CAA, the EPA has promulgated NAAQS for certain pollutants, including PM 2.5 . When the EPA promulgates a new NAAQS, CAA section 107 specifies a process for the designation of each area within a State, generally as either an area attaining the standard or as a nonattainment area (NAA) not attaining the standard or contributing to the nonattainment of the standard in a nearby area. CAA section 110 requires that each State adopt and submit to the EPA for approval a plan to provide for implementation, enforcement, and maintenance of the NAAQS. This plan is referred to as an infrastructure SIP. CAA section 110 also contains SIP requirements that must be met by each plan for the EPA's approval. SIPs usually include control measures to address emissions of air pollutants subject to the NAAQS from various sources including stationary, area, and mobile sources. CAA section 110(l) requires that any further revision of a State's adopted and effective SIP shall not be approved by the EPA if the revision would interfere with any applicable requirement of the CAA. II. Background On October 17, 2006, the EPA revised the 24-hour PM 2.5 NAAQS, lowering the primary and secondary standards to 35 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m 3 ). 1 On November 13, 2009, the EPA designated three areas in Utah as Moderate nonattainment for the 2006 24-hour PM 2.5 standard, including the Logan nonattainment area. 2 The Logan nonattainment area is composed of portions of Franklin County, in the State of Idaho, and Cache County, in the State of Utah. 1 71 FR 61144 (Oct. 17, 2006). 2 74 FR 58688 (Nov. 13, 2009). Through Utah's development of an attainment demonstration for the 24-hour PM 2.5 NAAQS, the State identified an I/M program implemented by Cache County as a reasonable control measure to achieve ambient PM 2.5 reductions via the reduction of small-diameter particulate matter precursor emissions of oxides of nitrogen (NO X ) and volatile organic compounds (VOC). Idaho did not identify a vehicle I/M program as a reasonable control measure for the Idaho portion of the Logan nonattainment area, given that the Idaho portion of the area contains roughly only 10 percent of the designated area's population base and overall mobile source emissions. 3 The Cache County I/M program was developed and fully implemented on January 1, 2014, under the direction of Cache County's local public health agency, the Bear River Health Department (BRHD). The Governor of Utah submitted a SIP revision to the EPA on January 28, 2014, to add the Cache County I/M program to the SIP under section X, part F. This SIP revision was approved by the EPA on September 9, 2015. 4 The Cache County I/M program is not required by the CAA subparts outlining general provisions for SIPs or additional provisions for particulate matter SIPs. Therefore, the Cache County program was developed using Federal I/M program requirements as a general model for program design, but the program is not held strictly to the EPA's I/M program requirements found in the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) in 40 CFR part 51, subpart S (hereafter, 40 CFR 51, subpart S) by the 2015 Cache County I/M program approval. For example, the Cache County program was not required to submit performance standard modeling to demonstrate equivalency to the I/M program performance standards for mandatory programs found in 40 CFR 51, subpart S. 5 After initial approval of the I/M program into the Utah SIP, the EPA evaluates proposed revisions to the Cache County I/M program pursuant to CAA section 110(l) requirements, evaluating whether the proposed program changes are part of a SIP revision that would result in the same emissions reduction benefits as compared to the status quo program. 6 3 78 FR 78315 (Dec. 26, 2013) and 82 FR 729 (Jan. 4, 2017). 4 80 FR 54237 (Sept. 9, 2015). 5 See 40 CFR 51.352(e)(13). 6 Id. On November 23, 2018, the EPA approved the Cache County I/M program as an “additional reasonable measure” under CAA section 172(c)(6) and the EPA's PM 2.5 Implementation Rule for timely attainment of the 24-hour PM 2.5 standard. 7 8 On May 19, 2021, the EPA approved redesignation of the Logan area to attainment status for the 2006 24-hour PM 2.5 NAAQS, the associated maintenance plan for the Utah portion of the Logan NAA, and related revisions to the SIP, including modifications of the Cache County I/M program. 9 7 83 FR 59315 (Nov. 23, 2018). 8 81 FR 58010 (Aug. 24, 2016). 9 86 FR 27035 (May 19, 2021). In a letter dated February 28, 2025, the Governor of Utah submitted a revision to section X, part F of the SIP. The revision reflects recent changes to the Cache County ordinances which define and implement the I/M program. Materials submitted with the Governor's letter constitute the State's showing that the SIP, as revised, accurately reflects the County's I/M program and does not reduce the stringency of the I/M program and that the program remains an additional reasonable measure of emissions reductions similar to the program as previously approved under CAA section 172(c)(6) and the PM 2.5 Implementation Rule for maintenance of the PM 2.5 NAAQS. 10 The EPA's review and evaluation of the submitted SIP revision and demonstration of compliance with CAA requirements is discussed in section III of this preamble. 10 81 FR 58010 (Aug. 24, 2016). III. The EPA's Evaluation of the State's Submittal A. Utah's SIP Revision When a Utah SIP is amended by the Utah Air Quality Board (UAQB), the amended sections must be incorporated into the Utah Air Quality Rules within the Utah Administrative Code. Utah incorporates SIP sections into the State's Rule R307-110. These rules are amended as needed to change the effective dates to match the UAQB approval date of various amendments to the Utah SIP. In this proposed action, the EPA is proposing to approve submitted revisions to Rule R307-110-36, which incorporates by reference (IBR) section X, Vehicle Inspection and Maintenance Program, part F, Cache County. Such IBR actions update incorporation of the State's general summary and basis of Cache County's I/M program, the County's authorizing ordinance for an I/M program, and the most recently adopted version of the BRHD's regulations defining the Cache County I/M program into State regulations which are all contained within the Utah SIP at section X.F. The EPA's evaluation of this revision follows. 1. R307-110-36 Section R307-110-36 incorporates the amendments to Utah SIP section X, Vehicle Inspection and Maintenance Program, part F, Cache County, into State rules, thereby making them effective as a matter of State law. The revision to R307-110-36 discussed in this preamble is a ministerial provision, which only revises the effective date within the rule to February 5, 2025, and does not itself include any control measures. The EPA evaluated the Governor's February 28, 2025, submitted revision to R307-110-36 based on the substantive revisions to the materials incorporated under that rule, as described below. 2. Section X, Vehicle Inspection and Maintenance Program, Part F, Cache County Section X, part F of the Utah SIP addresses the requirements for the implementation of the Cache County I/M program under the direction of the BRHD. Section X, part F contains three main components for the Cache County I/M program: (1) An outline setting forth program applicability, the general description of the program, and the required timeframe for its full implementation; (2) Cache County Ordinance 2013-04 which provides County-level authority to implement an I/M program and delegates implementation and administration of the program to the BRHD under general provisions and guidelines defined by the County; and (3) the BRHD's Regulation No. 2013-1 which fully defines the I/M program requirements, standards, and procedures. All substantive changes to the Cache County I/M program submitted to the EPA for review and approval with the Utah Governor's February 28, 2025, letter are found in the BRHD's Regulation No. 2013-1 as updated and adopted on July 1, 2024. The EPA's evaluation focuses on all substantive changes to Regulation No. 2013-1 as outlined and discussed below. i. Change of Definition In Regulation No. 2013-1, in the “Definitions” section, the BRHD amended the section by revising the definition of “I/M Program Station” by removing the word “stationary” as a necessary qualifier for I/M stations. All other requirements for inspection station qualification and licensure were left in the definition intact. The removal of “stationary” from the definition for an I/M program station in Cache County was made to allow for “mobile” emissions testing ( i.e., emissions testing performed by a qualified and permitted tester away from fixed, physical testing locations or facilities). This change allows for more flexible program operations following a successful mobile testing pilot program in 2023. The EPA's evaluation of this change to the regulatory definitions concludes that this revision is administrative in nature because it will not impact the emission reduction benefits of the Cache County I/M program. The “mobile” testing allowed by this change promotes motorist convenience and does not affect the subject vehicle population size, or the inspection station and inspector requirements the EPA has previously approved for the Cache County I/M program. The EPA's evaluation is that this revision to Regulation No. 2013-1 is administrative in nature and does not change the stringency of the Cache County I/M program or the emission reduction benefits produced by the program. ii. Emergency Vehicle Exemptions In Regulation No. 2013-1, in the “General Provisions” section, the BRHD amended sub-section 6.4, which covers vehicles exempt from the I/M program, by adding an exemption for any in-use “authorized emergency vehicle” as defined by the Utah Code. 11 Under the Utah Code, “authorized emergency vehicles” are defined as fire department vehicles, police vehicles, ambulances, and any other publicly or privately owned vehicles specially designated by the Department of Public Safety as an emergency vehicle. Thus, these four categories of emergency vehicles are exempted from the I/M program requirements under this revision. 11 Utah Code Annotated 41-6a-102. The EPA's evaluation of this revision focused on whether any emission reductions disbenefits were likely to result from the exemption or would interfere with maintenance of the 2006 24-hour PM 2.5 NAAQS or any other applicable requirement of the CAA. The model I/M program requirements under 40 CFR 51, subpart S state that SIP revisions granting exemptions to vehicles describe such special exemptions and give an estimate of the percentage and type of vehicles which will be granted special exemptions and account for the exemption within the program's quantitative emission reduction analysis. 12 Within the submittal, Utah includes an account of the number of vehicles affected by this exemption and the most recent estimate of total subject vehicles. In the SIP submittal, the State and Cache County indicated that this revision will exempt 102 emergency vehicles out of the 124,718 total vehicles registered in the county, or 0.08 percent of all registered vehicles. However, as noted previously in this document, the Cache County I/M program is not a mandatory program under the requirements of the CAA and was, therefore, not held strictly to the EPA's 40 CFR 51, subpart S requirements to quantify the change in emissions reduction benefits produced by the proposed exemption of emergency vehicles. The EPA, however, can qualitatively assess that an exemption of such a small proportion of the total vehicle fleet subject to I/M program testing would result in a nearly negligible change in emissions reductions, and an even more attenuated change in air quality benefits. Further, since it is best practice for maximum operational readiness that public safety agencies keep emergency vehicles properly maintained at all times (and not wait for periodic inspections to identify needed repairs), the EPA believes that there is little to no additional emission reduction benefit to be gained from conducting an inspection on a small number of emergency vehicles once every two years through the Cache County I/M program. The EPA discusses the qualitative impact of this exemption with respect to noninterference and approvability with more detail in section IV of this preamble, below. 12 40 CFR 51.356(b). The EPA's evaluation is that this revision to Regulation No. 2013-1 is consistent with Federal I/M program requirements and the exemption does not appreciably change the stringency of the Cache County I/M program or reduce the emissions reduction benefits produced by the program. iii. Parts Unavailability Waiver In Regulation No. 2013-1, the BRHD has amended the regulation by adding an Appendix G—“Waivers for Part Unavailability” which establishes conditions for issuance of a testing certification waiver based on unavailability of an essential component due to discontinuation of the manufacture of the component or for some other documented supply-chain issue. In order to qualify for the waiver, the unavailability of parts must be documented by the program and include certifications from two licensed and certified inspection stations. Part unavailability waivers under this added appendix are subject to other previously approved waiver conditions found elsewhere in the Cache County I/M program regulations. By the account of the State and Cache County's submittal, this revision may result in no more than 10 additional waivers per year. For reference, the BRHD reported to the EPA the issuance of zero waivers, for any reason, during the 2025 recordkeeping and reporting period. 13 Accordingly, the new waiver provision is not likely to result in an appreciable impact on the emissions reduction benefits of the I/M program. 13 See docket item: Cache CY2025 40 CFR 51.366(a)(2)(v). The EPA's evaluation of this revision focused on whether this revision satisfies the applicable requirements of CAA section 175A for maintenance plans and the applicable requirements for PM 2.5 control measures in CAA section 172(c)(6) and the EPA's PM 2.5 Implementation Rule. The parts unavailability waiver provision is a minor revision to a SIP-approved control measure which is not expected to appreciably change the stringency of the I/M program or change emission reduction benefits. Accordingly, the EPA proposes that the revised program will still meet all applicable requirements of CAA section 172(c)(6) and the EPA's Implementation Rule. As noted previously, the Cache County I/M program is not a CAA-mandated program and is, therefore, not required to meet the Federal I/M rule in 40 CFR 51, subpart S. Still, the EPA notes that parts unavailability waivers are even permissible pursuant to 40 CFR 51.360 of the Federal I/M rule. The EPA's evaluation is that this revision to Regulation No. 2013-1 is consistent with Federal I/M program requirements and the parts unavailability waiver does not appreciably change the stringency of the Cache County I/M program or reduce the emission reduction benefits produced by the program. IV. Consideration of Section 110(l) of the Clean Air Act Section 110(l) of the CAA states that a SIP revision cannot be approved if the revision interferes with any applicable requirement concerning attainment and reasonable further progress towards attainment of a NAAQS or any other applicable requirement of the CAA. The revisions to Utah SIP section X.F described in the previous section of this document provoke varied levels of consideration as relates to CAA section 110(l). The revision to “I/M Program Station” to allow for “mobile” emissions testing does not change the stringency of program requirements for test standards, program audits or inspector, testing equipment certification, or any other program element relevant to the program's emissions reduction efficacy. Accordingly, the EPA is proposing that this revision is administrative in nature and will not interfere with attainment, reasonable further progress, or any other applicable requirement of the CAA. The revision to the I/M program to exempt emergency vehicles impacts a small portion of the vehicles on the road in Cache County subject to emissions testing. Specifically, Cache County vehicle registrations sum to 124,718 vehicles, of which only 102 are emergency vehicles subject to this exemption. 14 This amounts to 0.08 percent of the County's registered vehicles. Exempting these 102 vehicles from emissions testing is expected to result in a negligible increase in emissions of pollutants subject to the NAAQS. Additionally, it is reasonable to assume that such emergency vehicles are well-maintained and repaired immediately when necessary. Thus, requiring the small population of emergency vehicles to participate in the bi-annual onboard diagnostic system check that is required as part of Cache County's I/M program would provide little to no additional emissions reductions benefit and exemption of those vehicles from the checks is acceptable. 14 See docket item: “CAA section 110(l) Demonstration”. The State also provided in its CAA section 110(l) analysis a summary of the area's 3-year air quality design values for the 10 years prior to this SIP submittal. 15 16 The most recent design value reported in the State's CAA section 110(l) demonstration is 30.6 µg/m 3 for the three years centered on 2024, well below the standard of 35 µg/m 3 . The design values for the area do not suggest that the small-to-negligible disbenefit that would result from exempting emergency vehicles from the I/M program would interfere with maintenance of the NAAQS. The EPA concludes that any potential increases in emissions from this small number of emergency vehicles will not interfere with the attainment, reasonable further progress, or any other applicable requirements of the CAA. 15 Id. 16 See 40 CFR Appendix N to Part 50 1.0(c) “Design values (DVs)”. The addition of a parts unavailability waiver to the Cache County I/M program provides operational flexibility and an adaptation to supply chain difficulties without conflicting with the EPA's I/M program requirements. The EPA expects the parts unavailability waiver would be applicable to only a relatively small portion of the vehicle fleet subject to the program and will not likely change the acceptable program waiver rate associated with maintenance of the 2006 24-hr PM 2.5 NAAQS. If the waiver rate for the Cache County program increases notably after implementation of the new waiver category, the County is obligated to document the trend in annual reporting to the EPA and will need to adjust I/M program requirements accordingly. 17 The EPA proposes that the parts unavailability waiver will not interfere with attainment, reasonable further progress, or any other applicable requirement of the CAA. 17 See Utah SIP, section X.A: General Requirements Vehicle Inspection and Maintenance Program, section 3. General Summary, Data analysis and reporting requirements. V. Incorporation by Reference In this document, the EPA is proposing to include regulatory text in a final rule that includes incorporation by reference. In accordance with requirements of 1 CFR 51.5, the EPA is proposing to incorporate by reference revisions to R307-110-36 and Utah SIP section X.F, as discussed in Sections III. and IV. of this preamble. The EPA has made, and will continue to make, these materials generally available through https://www.regulations.gov and at the EPA Region 8 Office (please contact the person identified in the FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT section of this preamble for more information). VI. Statutory and Executive Order Reviews Under the CAA the Administrator is required to approve a SIP submission that complies with the provisions of the CAA and applicable Federal regulations (42 U.S.C. 7410(k); 40 CFR 52.02(a)). Thus, in reviewing SIP submissions, the EPA's role is to approve State choices, provided that they meet the criteria of the CAA. Accordingly, this action merely proposes to approve State law as meeting Federal requirements and does not impose additional requirements beyond those imposed by State law. For that reason, this action: • Is not a “significant regulatory action” subject to review by the Office of Management and Budget under Executive Orders 12866 (58 FR 51735, October 4, 1993); • Is not an Executive Order 14192 (90 FR 9065, February 6, 2025) regulatory action because this action is not significant under Executive Order 12866; • Does not impose an information collection burden under the provisions of the Paperwork Reduction Act (44 U.S.C. 3501 et seq. ); • Is certified as not having a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities under the Regulatory Flexibility Act (5 U.S.C. 601 et seq. ); • Does not contain any unfunded mandate or significantly or uniquely affect small governments, as described in the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (Pub. L. 104-4); • Does not have federalism implications as specified in Executive Order 13132 (64 FR 43255, August 10, 1999); • Is not subject to Executive Order 13045 (62 FR 19885, April 23, 1997) because it approves a State program; • Is not a significant regulatory action subject to Executive Order 13211 (66 FR 28355, May 22, 2001); and • Is not subject to requirements of section 12(d) of the National Technology Transfer and Advancement Act of 1995 (15 U.S.C. 272 note) because application of those requirements would be inconsistent with the Clean Air Act. In addition, the SIP is not approved to apply on any Indian reservation land or in any other area where the EPA or an Indian Tribe has demonstrated that a Tribe has jurisdiction. In those areas of Indian country, the proposed rule does not have Tribal implications and will not impose substantial direct costs on Tribal governments or preempt Tribal law as specified by Executive Order 13175 (65 FR 67249, November 9, 2000). title: Air Plan Approval; Texas; Attainment Plan for the Navarro County 2010 Sulfur Dioxide Primary National Ambient Air Quality Standard Nonattainment Area
content: ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY 40 CFR Part 52 [EPA-R06-OAR-2024-0069; FRL-13714-01-R6] Air Plan Approval; Texas; Attainment Plan for the Navarro County 2010 Sulfur Dioxide Primary National Ambient Air Quality Standard Nonattainment Area AGENCY: Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). ACTION: Proposed rule. SUMMARY: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is proposing to approve the State Implementation Plan (SIP) revision that Texas submitted to the EPA on October 24, 2022, for the 2010 1-hour sulfur dioxide (SO 2 ) primary national ambient air quality standard (NAAQS) in the Navarro County SO 2 nonattainment area. This SIP (or “attainment plan”) includes Texas' attainment demonstration provisions and emissions inventory for the nonattainment area, demonstration of reasonable further progress (RFP), implementation of reasonably available control measures (RACM) (including reasonably available control technology (RACT)), an approved nonattainment new source review (NNSR) program, enforceable emissions limitations and control measures, and adequate contingency measures for the affected area. The EPA is proposing to approve Texas' attainment plan for Navarro County and accompanying provisions for the enforceable control strategy for the Navarro area. Reasonably Available Control Measures and Reasonably Available Control Technology (RACM/RACT) C. Nonattainment New Source Review (NSR) D. Reasonable Further Progress (RFP) E. Contingency Measures F. Conformity VII. Proposed Action VIII. Incorporation by Reference IX. Statutory and Executive Order Reviews I. Executive Summary A. What action is the EPA taking? The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is proposing to approve Texas' October 24, 2022, State Implementation Plan (SIP) submittal demonstrating the plan for attainment of the 2010 1-hour sulfur dioxide (SO 2 ) primary national ambient air quality standard (NAAQS) for the Navarro County nonattainment area (Navarro NAA). As part of this proposed action, the EPA is also proposing to approve and incorporate by reference into the State's SIP, a portion of the October 24, 2022, Texas rulemaking SIP revision containing Texas' recently adopted provisions at Texas Administrative Code Title 30, Chapter 112: Control of Air Pollution from Sulfur Compounds, Subchapter G: Requirements in the Navarro County Nonattainment Area (30 TAC 112, subchapter G), that provide the enforceable control strategy for the Navarro NAA. B. What is the legal authority and what are the requirements? The EPA's regulations governing nonattainment area SIPs are set forth at 40 CFR part 51, with specific procedural requirements and control strategy requirements at subparts F and G, respectively. State attainment plans are approved by the EPA as meeting the minimum requirements of the Clean Air Act (CAA or Act) if they fully address the requirements of CAA sections 110, 172, 191 and 192, and the EPA's regulations at 40 CFR part 51. The EPA is proposing to find that Texas' attainment plan for the Navarro NAA meets these requirements. II. Background Under CAA section 109, the EPA has established primary and secondary NAAQS for certain air pollutants (referred to as “criteria pollutants”) and conducts periodic reviews of the NAAQS to determine whether they should be revised or whether new NAAQS should be established. On June 22, 2010, the EPA promulgated a new 1-hour primary SO 2 NAAQS of 75 parts per billion (ppb) at 40 CFR 50.17(a), which is met at an ambient air quality monitoring site when the 3-year average of the annual 99th percentile of daily maximum 1-hour average concentrations does not exceed 75 ppb, as determined in accordance with Appendix T of 40 CFR part 50. 1 Under CAA section 107(d)(1), the EPA is required to designate areas as “nonattainment,” “attainment,” or “unclassifiable” within two years of establishing a new or revised standard. The Navarro NAA for the 2010 SO 2 NAAQS was established effective April 30, 2021. 2 3 This final designation triggered a requirement for Texas to submit, by October 30, 2022 (within 18 months per CAA section 191(a)), a SIP revision with a plan for how the Navarro NAA would attain the 2010 SO 2 NAAQS as expeditiously as practicable, but no later than April 30, 2026. 1 See 75 FR 35520 (June 22, 2010). 2 See 86 FR 16055 (March 26, 2021). See also 40 CFR part 81, subpart C. 3 On August 21, 2015 (80 FR 51052), EPA promulgated air quality characterization requirements for the 2010 1-hour SO 2 NAAQS in the Data Requirements Rule (DRR). The DRR requires State air agencies to characterize air quality, through air dispersion modeling or monitoring, in areas associated with sources that emitted in 2014 2,000 tons per year (tpy) or more of SO 2 , or that have otherwise been listed under the DRR by EPA or state air agencies. EPA used the information generated by implementation of the DRR to help inform the 2021 designations ( See 86 FR 16055, March 26, 2021) for the 2010 1-hour SO 2 NAAQS. The 2021 designations were based primarily on ambient monitoring data, including data from existing and new EPA-approved monitors that have collected data at least from January 2017 forward, pursuant to the DRR. Texas submitted an attainment plan for the Navarro NAA on October 24, 2022. This notice describes the requirements that the attainment plan must meet under the CAA in order for the EPA to approve the provisions into the federally enforceable SIP, provides a review of the State's plan for attainment with respect to these requirements, and describes the EPA's proposed action on the attainment plan. III. Requirements for SO 2 Attainment Plans The nonattainment area SIP for SO 2 must meet the applicable requirements of CAA sections 110, 172, 191 and 192. The EPA's regulations governing nonattainment area SIPs are set forth at 40 CFR part 51, with specific procedural requirements and control strategy requirements at subparts F and G, respectively. Soon after Congress enacted the 1990 amendments to the CAA, the EPA issued guidance on SIPs in the document “General Preamble for the Implementation of Title I of the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990,” (General Preamble). 4 Among other things, the General Preamble addressed requirements for SO 2 SIPs and fundamental principles for SIP control strategies. 5 On April 23, 2014, the EPA issued guidance and recommendations for meeting the statutory requirements in SIPs addressing the 2010 1-hour primary SO 2 NAAQS, in a document entitled “Guidance for 1-Hour SO 2 Nonattainment Area SIP Submissions” (hereafter referred to as “2014 SO 2 Nonattainment Guidance”). 6 In this guidance, the EPA described the statutory requirements for the elements of a nonattainment area SIP as listed at CAA section 172(c), which include: an accurate emissions inventory of current emissions for all sources of SO 2 within the nonattainment area; an attainment demonstration; demonstration of RFP; RACM including RACT; enforceable emission limitations and control measures necessary to provide for attainment; nonattainment new source review (NNSR); and adequate contingency measures. 4 See 57 FR 13498 (April 16, 1992) 5 Id. at 57 FR 13545 through 13549; 57 FR 13567 through 13568. 6 Available in the docket for this proposed action and at https://www.epa.gov/sites/production/files/2016-06/documents/20140423guidance_nonattainment_sip.pdf. In general, the EPA's duties for reviewing State attainment plans are described in CAA sections 110(k) and 110(l). Pursuant to CAA section 110(k)(1), the EPA must first determine if a SIP submission meets certain minimum criteria for administrative completeness. Once a SIP submission has been determined to be complete, the EPA shall approve the submission as a whole if it meets all applicable requirements of the CAA. State attainment plans must satisfy the relevant statutory and regulatory criteria found in CAA sections 110, 172, 191 and 192, and the EPA's regulations at 40 CFR part 51 in order to be approved by the EPA. Also, under CAA section 110(l), the EPA may not approve a SIP revision that would interfere with any applicable requirement concerning NAAQS attainment and RFP, or any other applicable requirement of the CAA. Further, under CAA section 193, no control requirement in effect before November 15, 1990 (or required to be adopted by an order, settlement, agreement, or plan in effect before November 15, 1990), in any area which is a nonattainment area for any air pollutant, may be modified in any manner unless the modification insures equivalent or greater emission reductions of such air pollutant. CAA sections 172(c)(1) and 172(c)(6) direct States with areas designated as nonattainment to demonstrate that the submitted attainment plan and its emission limitations and control measures provide for attainment of the NAAQS. 40 CFR part 51, subpart G further delineates the control strategy requirements that SIPs must meet, and that all SIPs and control strategies reflect the four fundamental principles of quantification, enforceability, replicability, and accountability. 7 SO 2 attainment plans must consist of two components: (1) enforceable emission limits and other control measures that assure implementation of permanent, enforceable and necessary emission controls, and (2) a modeling analysis which meets the requirements of 40 CFR part 51, Appendix W (Appendix W) and demonstrates that necessary emission limits and control measures provide for timely attainment of the primary SO 2 NAAQS as expeditiously as practicable, but by no later than the attainment date for the affected area. In all cases, these emission limits and control measures must be accompanied by appropriate methods and conditions to determine compliance with the respective emission limits and control measures, and must be quantifiable ( i.e., a specific amount of emission reduction can be ascribed to the measures), fully enforceable (specifying clear, unambiguous and measurable requirements for which compliance can be practicably determined), replicable (the procedures for determining compliance are sufficiently specific and non-subjective so that two independent entities applying the procedures would obtain the same result), and accountable (source-specific limits must be permanent and must reflect the assumptions used in the SIP demonstrations). 7 See General Preamble; 57 FR 13498, April 16, 1992 at 57 FR 13567 through 13568. Preferred air quality models for use in regulatory applications are described in Addendum A of the EPA's Guideline on Air Quality Models (40 CFR part 51, Appendix W). In 2005, the EPA promulgated the American Meteorological Society/Environmental Protection Agency Regulatory Model (AERMOD) 8 as the Agency's preferred near-field dispersion modeling for a wide range of regulatory applications addressing stationary sources (for example in estimating SO 2 concentrations) in all types of terrain based on extensive developmental and performance evaluations. 9 Supplemental guidance on modeling for purposes of demonstrating attainment of the SO 2 standard is provided in Appendix A to the 2014 SO 2 Nonattainment Guidance. Appendix A of the 2014 SO 2 Nonattainment Guidance provides extensive guidance on the modeling domain, the source inputs, assorted types of meteorological data, and background concentrations. 8 American Meteorological Society (AMS)/EPA Regulatory Model. The modeling system includes the AERMOD model itself, along with the required preprocessors and their components. 9 See 70 FR 68218 (Nov. 9, 2005). Attainment demonstrations for the 2010 1-hour primary SO 2 NAAQS must demonstrate future attainment of the NAAQS in the entire area designated as nonattainment ( i.e., not just at the violating monitor) by using air quality dispersion modeling ( see Appendix W to 40 CFR part 51) to show that the mix of sources and enforceable control measures and emission rates in an identified area will not lead to a violation of the SO 2 NAAQS. For a short-term ( i.e., 1-hour) standard, the EPA finds that dispersion modeling, using allowable emissions and addressing stationary sources in the affected area (and sources located outside the nonattainment area which may affect attainment in the area, if applicable) is technically appropriate, efficient, and effective in demonstrating attainment in nonattainment areas, because it takes into consideration combinations of meteorological and emission source operating conditions that may contribute to peak ground-level concentrations of SO 2. Resultant model-predicted concentrations for NAAQS demonstrations should always include ambient background concentrations added to explicitly modeled concentrations, should follow the form of the standard, and should be calculated as described in section 2.6.1.2 of the August 23, 2010, clarification memo on “Applicability of Appendix W Modeling Guidance for the 1-hour SO 2 National Ambient Air Quality Standard” (Modeling Guideline). 10 10 S ee Clarification Memo Appendix W Hourly SO 2 (August 23, 2010) in the docket for this proposed action. IV. Summary of Texas' SIP Submission On March 26, 2021, the EPA designated a portion of Navarro County, Texas as nonattainment for the 2010 1-hour primary SO 2 NAAQS, effective April 30, 2021. 11 During the 2017-2019 design value period, the nearby Richland Southeast 1220 Road monitor (AQS ID# 48-349-1081) violated the NAAQS with a monitored design value of 165 ppb. The primary major source of emissions in the area is the Arcosa Lightweight Streetman Plant (Streetman Plant) which manufactures lightweight aggregate for use in various industrial applications such as concrete and asphalt. 11 See 86 FR 16055 See also 40 CFR part 81, subpart C. CAA section 191 directs States to submit SIPs for nonattainment areas to the EPA within 18 months of the effective date of the designation, i.e., by no later than October 30, 2022, for the Navarro NAA. Under CAA section 192, these SIPs are required to demonstrate that their respective nonattainment areas will attain the NAAQS as expeditiously as practicable, but no later than 5 years from the effective date of designation, i.e., April 30, 2026. Texas held a public hearing concerning the Navarro County attainment demonstration on May 23, 2022. No members of the public attended the public hearing. Texas adopted the attainment demonstration on October 5, 2022. On October 24, 2022, Texas submitted the attainment plan for the Navarro NAA to the EPA. In addition to the attainment demonstration, Texas submitted the newly adopted sections of State regulations in 30 TAC 112, subchapter G. These regulations contain the enforceable control strategy which is incorporated into the attainment plan for the Navarro NAA. V. Review of Modeled Attainment Plan This section discusses the EPA's review and analysis of the modeled attainment plan, including model selection, meteorological data, emissions data, receptor grid, emissions limits, and background concentrations. A more detailed discussion is presented in a technical support document (TSD) contained in the public docket for this proposed approval of the Texas SIP revision. A. Model Selection and General Model Inputs As part of its SIP development process, Texas used the EPA's regulatory dispersion model, AERMOD, to determine the SO 2 emission reductions and stack modifications needed to bring the Navarro NAA into attainment. Texas relied upon AERMOD Version 21112 and the companion AERMOD User Guide documentation in developing the attainment demonstration for the Navarro NAA. Regulatory default options were specified in developing the attainment demonstration that are consistent with established practices for use of AERMOD in determining NAAQS compliance for SIP revisions. Included among those default options are stack tip downwash, buoyancy induced dispersion, default wind profile coefficients, default vertical potential temperature gradients, and final plume rise. The EPA finds these selections appropriate. This attainment demonstration uses a modeling domain that reflects the geographic extent of the Navarro NAA. The most significant source, and only point source, addressed in the modeling for the area is the Streetman Plant facility. A review of industrial SO 2 sources within and near the nonattainment area indicates that this facility is the primary contributor to the monitored violations. At the highest concentrations modeled in the area by the attainment demonstration modeling submitted by TCEQ, the Streetman Plant contributed more than 99% in total to the modeled SO 2 concentrations. The way this source was modeled is discussed later in this section. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) followed 40 CFR part 51 Appendix W, Guideline on Air Quality Models, and the EPA's 2014 SO 2 Attainment Demonstration Guidance in utilizing the AERMOD modeling system pre-processors to generate AERMOD-ready files for meteorology (via AERMET and AERMINUTE), and terrain and elevation (via AERMAP and AERSURFACE). The Streetman Plant was required by TCEQ's chapter 112 Rule to construct a new stack to replace the existing kiln stack no later than January 1, 2025. The chapter 112 Rule specifies that the stack was to be built at a height at least 120 feet (36.6 meters), specifies the location of the stack and identifies the emission limit, minimum stack temperature and minimum stack exit gas velocity. The EPA's Appendix W guidance indicates that States should evaluate whether physical structures may affect the dispersion of emissions from stack sources. Stacks that are constructed to heights lower than specified Good Engineering Practice (GEP) height 12 and within the “zone of influence” of a nearby structure have plumes that are potentially subject to the effects of downwash which would affect dispersion and modeled concentrations in the building wake, near to the source. TCEQ used site-specific building and stack data and modeled the stack at the Streetman Plant to comply with GEP stack height requirements. TCEQ used the EPA's Building Profile Input Program with PRIME algorithm (BPIPPRM) to generate direction-specific building parameters for modeling building wake effects. The location and height of the new stack, and the locations and heights of nearby structures, were processed in BPIPPRM (version 04274) to produce the building downwash parameters required by AERMOD. The actual release height of the stack was less than the GEP value. Therefore, the new stack at the Streetman plant was modeled at the actual release height and was analyzed for downwash effects of the plumes within AERMOD. The EPA is proposing to determine that TCEQ's application of the modeling guideline is appropriate for addressing stacks subject to downwash effects and that the new stack built at the Streetman Plant complies with GEP stack height requirements. 12 40 CFR 51.100(ii) defines GEP stack height limits. In the accompanying TSD, the EPA provides further explanation and review of Texas' meteorological fields, receptor grid, building downwash, model settings and other model inputs, as well as other details used to develop the modeling demonstration. The EPA finds that TCEQ's model selection, development of modeling input files and selection of general inputs for its model conform with the EPA's modeling requirements and guidance. B. Meteorological Data The State's modeling utilized surface meteorological data obtained from then-most recent five years (2015 through2020) 13 of available surface meteorological data from Corsicana, Texas (Weather Bureau Army Navy (WBAN) No. 53912, 14 kilometers to the north-northwest of the Streetman Plant) and coincident upper air data from Shreveport, Louisiana (WBAN No. 13957, 247 km to the east-northeast of the Streetman Plant). The Corsicana, Texas station is the closest National Weather Service (NWS) site to the Streetman Plant, and the Shreveport, Louisiana station was chosen by Texas as best representative of meteorological conditions within the area of analysis due to proximity, similar terrain, and availability of recently collected data. The EPA recommends using the closest NWS sites for surface and upper air data if they are considered representative of the area being modeled. In this situation, the EPA concurs with the use of these two sites for this modeling as meeting the EPA's criteria as being nearby and representative. The EPA also finds that TCEQ adequately processed the data in accordance with the Modeling Guideline and the EPA's guidance to generate the necessary modeling data to be used in the AERMOD model runs. In the accompanying TSD, the EPA provides further details and analysis of our review of Texas' meteorological data and AERMET and AERMINUTE settings that were used for processing the meteorological data for use in AERMOD. The EPA is proposing to find the selection and processing of this data to be appropriate and in accordance with Appendix W and the 2014 SO 2 Nonattainment Guidance. 13 At the surface station, the fourth quarter of meteorological data did not meet EPA's data completeness requirements in 2018 and thus 2018 was excluded from the meteorological processing. As such, the next available year, 2015, was subsitituted. C. Emissions Data As detailed in the SIP submission, Texas identified the Streetman Plant as the most significant source affecting the Navarro NAA, the sole major point source of SO 2 . There are no other minor or major SO 2 point sources in the nonattainment area contributing to the monitored violations. Other impacts of SO 2 emissions from non-point sources, for example mobile source emissions, incineration, agricultural field burning, etc., were not explicitly modeled in AERMOD but instead represented via monitored background data. Texas' SIP submittal describes an exploratory modeling run that the State conducted to identify the cause of the violations in the area and determine the most appropriate remedy. This modeling pointed to a single emissions source of SO 2 at the Streetman Plant: a kiln stack for a lightweight aggregate kiln, Emission Point Number (EPN) E3-1 (kiln stack). The State also evaluated the Guardian Industries' (located seven kilometers beyond the northern boundary of the nonattainment area with annual reported SO 2 emissions of 243 through 298 tpy) impact within the nonattainment area, and provided modeling results showing a small impact, and proposed to not explicitly model Guardian Industries' emissions. To address these violations, Texas chose to use modeling as a guide tool to arrive at the combination of emissions and stack parameters for a new stack and scrubber system that provided for attainment of the NAAQS. TCEQ ultimately decided on enforceable rules for these as discussed in the following paragraphs. The SIP and attainment demonstration modeling, submitted by the State, incorporate the new scrubber stack and operating conditions as necessary to attain the NAAQS according to the specific parameters and limitations of the new subchapter G of TCEQ's 30 TAC 112. The new scrubber stack must have vertical unobstructed stack release and be operated at all times with minimum values for temperature (117 degrees Fahrenheit), exit velocity (42.5 meters/second), and exhaust release height (at least 36.576 meters tall). Texas' AERMOD modeling estimated concentrations based on application of the TCEQ rule-required parameters and scrubber stack SO 2 emissions limit of 222 pounds per hour (lbs/hour), which is substantially lower than the kiln stack's previous permitted limit of 1,000 lbs/hour. A continuous emissions monitoring system (CEMS) is also required on this kiln stack to verify emissions compliance. The State also considered potential emissions during periods of startup, shutdown, and malfunction (SSM) when developing its attainment demonstration. Due to the source only utilizing natural gas as a fuel during periods of SSM, the estimated potential to emit during these periods is estimated to always be less than the hourly emissions under normal operating conditions; therefore, SSM scenarios will not result in higher modeled values than routine conditions, and are required to also be monitored by CEMS at these times. Additional details and evaluation of the other model inputs of Texas' attainment demonstration modeling, e.g., list of modeled sources and modeling parameters, are provided in the accompanying TSD. D. Receptor Grid Within AERMOD, air quality concentration results are calculated at discrete locations identified by the user; these locations are called receptors. TCEQ's modeling domain for this demonstration consisted of three nested receptor grids with high density receptor grids nearest the source and lesser density receptor grids further away from the Streetman Plant. The inner-most grid consists of a 7.0 km by 7.0 km square centered upon the Streetman Plant with a gridded receptor array at approximately 50-meter intervals. The middle grid extends from the 7.0 km nested, inner-most grid square to form a 14.4 km square with a gridded receptor array of 100-meter interval spacings. The outer-most grid extends from the 14.4 km middle grid square to the outermost edge of the nonattainment area with receptors spaced 500 meters apart. The EPA's 2014 SO 2 Nonattainment Guidance states that modeling for SO 2 attainment demonstrations must evaluate SO 2 concentrations across all areas within the nonattainment area “that are considered ambient air (where the public generally has access).” Receptors were excluded over the internal boundary of the Streetman Plant which is considered non-ambient air relative to its own emissions. Receptors were also added along the Streetman Plant property fence line at 25 meters spacing intervals, plus one additional receptor placed at the location of the Richland Southeast 1220 Road monitor. The EPA concurs that the receptor grid was adequate and also reviewed the documentation regarding areas determined to be non-ambient (not needing receptors). The TSD includes additional discussion of identification of receptors and areas considered non-ambient (restricted access), along with the EPA's related review and conclusions. E. Emission Limits As required by the Texas regulations found at 30 TAC 112, subchapter G, the SO 2 emissions of the scrubber stack shall not exceed 222 lbs/hr, the temperature of the exhaust gas exiting the stack may not fall below 117 degrees Fahrenheit, and the velocity of the exhaust gas exiting the stack may not drop below 42.5 feet/second.
